notes.urn:cts:latinLit:stoa0117.stoa008.opp-la: The scan has many errors, read as evident: e.g. 'palmus' for psalmus, 'abbatis .panibus' for abbatis manibus, 'autor pecuniæ' for amor pecuniae, 'casuum' for casum, 'furtisum' for furtivum. 'Ad virtutem iis suppetat ... coacii' read as coacti (gathered). 'Penicillus' (writing-brush/pen) and 'hemiphorium' (a short garment, sense uncertain) follow the edition.

§8: 'vitia' read as 'vilia' (cheap). §9: 'pater Muthius' taken as Patermutus (Cassian's Patermucius). §11: 'Pinophan' is Cassian's Pinufius; 'Panepho' taken as Panephysis; 'Non ponit' read as 'non potuit'; the Matthew reference is 5:14, not 5:15. §12: 'vel orantes' is obscure, perhaps for 'vel ignorantes' (even unknowingly); the unnamed Scripture is Eccles. 5:4; chapter range '33-55' read as 33–35. §13: the sentence 'Ubi psalterium didiceris... ne te transgressorem exhibeas' appears garbled or abridged (Cassian warns against pride over learning; cf. Gal. 2:18); the 'Matth. 5:19' reference fits Luke 9:62 better; Luke 12:31 is 12:32.

Line .14: 'ex scientia vitae' is odd and may be corrupt (perhaps for 'sententia' or 'proposito'); translated literally. 'Illud quartum' ('that fourth thing') refers to an item not clearly enumerated in this epitome. The bracketed Cassian variant on the ninth sign in line .13 is the edition's own insertion. Line .16: 'nec tamen viro sum' read as 'virgo sum' (I am not a virgin), as in Cassian's version of Basil's saying. Psalm and other references follow the Vulgate numbering as printed. The last line breaks off mid-sentence in the edition.

The edition splits this long passage across two lines under one reference; the break falls inside the citation of Acts 20:35. Several scanning errors are read as evident: 'segnifie' as segnitie (sloth), 'lepido' as tepido (lukewarm), 'serve- DIUS' as servemus, 'venit' as veni, 'Stulle' as Stulte, 'supra apostolos' as super apostolos. The opening sentence, 'Quandoquidem vero illud... male quidam interpretantur... sciant hujusmodi homines', is anacoluthic in the Latin and is rendered as it stands. 'Necessariis rebus nihil curamus' is taken as 'we have no care even about necessary things', that is, the monastery provides them.

'Vice eorum qui injuriarum memoriam tenent, ad mortem' is evidently corrupt for 'viae' (Prov. 12:28 LXX, cited by Cassian); translated as 'ways'. The edition's reference Prov. 12:25 is likely wrong. Some scripture references in the edition are also off (e.g. Luke 4:25 for 4:23, Mark 7:23 for Matt. 7:3–4, Matt. 5:4 for 5:24, Prov. 'SI, 25'); the corrected references are given. 'conchet' read as 'concitet'.

Section 6 begins mid-sentence after a lost leaf (noted in the text itself); 'Panem manducent' is the end of a quotation, probably 2 Thess. 3:12. The printed reference 'c. 43' is read as c. 13 (Cassian, Inst. X.13ff.); 'Proo. IV, 23' is read as Prov. 4:23; 'II Cor. SII, 2' as 2 Cor. 12:2. In section 5, 'spiritus nequitiæ' is taken as accusative plural ('the spirits of wickedness'). In section 7, 'quem non potuit honore' lacks a verb; '[puff up]' is supplied from the following clause.

'verba demersonis' read as 'verba demersionis' (words of drowning/ruin, Ps. 51:6 Vulg. 'verba praecipitationis'). 'Tu vero homo, et non Deus' is cited as Isa. 31:3 but matches Ezek. 28:2. 'a-id enim habes' read as 'Quid enim habes'. 'perveniro' read as 'pervenire'. The sentence 'But you are puffed up...' appears to be the epitomator's comment, not part of the Pauline quotation.

nodes.text: THE TWO BOOKS OF EPITOMES OF THE WORKS OF CASSIAN, BY SAINT EUCHERIUS, BISHOP OF LYON, TO CASTOR OF APT.
BOOK ONE.
ON THE CANONICAL INSTITUTES OF THE MONASTERIES.

1. (Cassian, Institutes, preface and book II, chapters 7–11.) Since you have bidden me, most blessed father Castor, to set out for you the canonical rules of the monasteries of the East, and above all of Egypt, which I saw with my own eyes, I have, in obedience to your command, sent you these few words, so that from them provision for the journey toward virtue may be at hand for those who, with God's help, have been gathered together in your new monastery. I have likewise sent the canons of the blessed men, and some others. It is necessary, then, that before all else I speak about prayer, the source of all good things: namely how, and in what excellent order, they perform it in the monasteries of Egypt and the Thebaid. For when they are gathered in one place at the time of the *synaxis* [assembly for prayer], after the psalm is finished they do not at once go down on their knees, but before they bend the knee they pray standing for a short time with hands outstretched; afterwards they prostrate themselves on the ground, and after a brief prayer made while kneeling, they all rise together; and again with hands outstretched they offer their supplications at greater length and more fervently, no one kneeling, or rising from kneeling, until the one who recites the prayer has knelt first, or risen first. So, as has been said, when they come together for such *synaxes*, such silence is kept by all that in so great and almost countless a gathering no one seems to be present; above all at the time of the prayers, when no one spits and no cough is heard: no sign of sloth is heard there, no dozing, no yawning, no audible groaning. For they say that one who prays aloud out of weariness and slackness of spirit sins doubly: first, because he prays sluggishly; second, because with that undisciplined voice he deafens his neighbour's ears and distracts his mind; and the evil spirits join in the attack, who, when they see us standing at prayer, weigh down the soul with unseemly thoughts and with weariness and disgust. This is the reason why they do not recite the psalms in haste, with noise and confusion, and do not take delight in a multitude of verses but in the attention of the mind: following, that is, in this thought him who says: I will sing with the spirit, I will sing also with the mind (1 Cor. 14:15); judging it more profitable to sing ten verses with attention than the whole psalter with confusion of mind. 2. (Cassian, Institutes, book II, chapter 15.) When the psalms and the canon are completed, as we mentioned above, none of the brothers dares to stand with another or talk for even the briefest time; nor to leave his cell, or abandon the work which he has in hand, according to the apostolic precept; unless on occasion of some necessary work they must all come together; and when they go out they carry out their work in such a way that there is not even the slightest conversation among them, but each gives himself to meditation of mind and to the psalm, and fulfils what he has been ordered. Further, they take great care that no brother is ever left alone with another, especially a novice, or dares to touch or embrace anyone with outstretched hands. And if anyone is caught transgressing this rule, he is subjected to a most severe rebuke.

3. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 1–6.) Concerning the canonical practice, then, whether of prayers or of psalms, that is, how they ought to be observed in the daily assemblies, enough has now been said by us; next we must treat of those who have renounced the world: on what terms they enter these monasteries, and remain in them in humility and obedience until extreme old age. For such obedience, such humility is found among them right up to old age, as is not found among those who have renounced the world in our monasteries even in their first year. So the man who wishes to be a monk is not admitted into the monastery before he has given some proof and trial of his love toward God, of his humility and patience, through the utmost obedience. Approved in these things, he is then held by them as fit to be admitted, and is taught not to keep anything of his goods stored away for himself: for they know that one who keeps back anything of his goods cannot long remain in the obedience of the monastery, nor persevere to the end, because of slackness and weariness of spirit. For when any slightest occasion or affliction stirs his mind, at once the hope of the hidden treasure throws him out of the monastery, as a sling throws a stone. Therefore each of them is stripped of his former possessions, so that he is not even allowed to use the garment he was wearing. But when all the brothers are gathered, he is led into their midst, stripped of his own clothes, and in their place is clothed by the abbot's hands in the clothes of the monastery; so that by this figure he himself may recognise that, stripped of all worldly things, and likewise of arrogance and pride, he has put on the poverty of Christ, and may without shame count and make himself equal with the body of the brotherhood. The clothes of which he is stripped the steward of the monastery takes and keeps, and puts aside separately, until he has made progress and given proof of his way of life and of patience in various temptations. And if he is found able to persevere in these things, and to remain in the zeal and fervent purpose with which he began, they count him among the rest of the brothers. But if they find in him the fault of murmuring, or the sin of any disobedience, they strip him of the monastery's clothes, dress him again in worldly garments, and expel him from the community. So after so careful a trial it is not easy for anyone at his own will either to enter or to leave the monastery; but whoever declares that he does not wish to remain is stripped entirely of the monastery's clothes.

4. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 7–9.) When, therefore, the one who has been received has been tested with the care we have described and found blameless, he is not at once allowed to mingle with the community of the brothers, but is handed over to the one entrusted with the care of guests, and is ordered to devote himself wholly to the service and attendance of guests; and after he has received guests blamelessly for a whole year, formed by this into humility and patience, he is at last counted among the community of the brothers, and is handed over to one of the elders who bears the responsibility of this office, to teach the disciple by what paths he may come to the perfection of the virtues. First of all he teaches him the practice of overcoming his own desires and pleasures, by ordering things contrary to his will. For the Fathers say that no one can otherwise curb pleasures, or anger, or sadness, or attain true humility, or finally be rightly perfected together with the brothers in the community, unless he has first put his own wishes to death through obedience. When by these rules and teachings, as by a kind of letters and syllables, they have brought the disciple on to a higher state, they next teach him not to hide his thoughts, but as soon as they come, to reveal them at once to his father; and not to trust his own heart in any judgement or examination of them, but to know that to be good, and that to be bad, which the father by his judgement, after examining the matter, has declared to be such. In this way anyone being trained in virtue will be able to avoid all the deceits of the enemy, inexperienced as he is and ignorant of the enemy's tricks. For the holy Fathers say that it is a clear sign of the devil's art and snares when he persuades disciples to hide their thoughts from their fathers, and this either out of a movement of pride, as though they themselves were fit to take suitable counsel on the matter by themselves, or out of vainglory, because of course they are ashamed to make their thoughts known.

5. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 10–12.) Moreover such is their obedience that without the abbot's command no one dares even to go out of the cell in which he sits; and they carry out his commands with as much zeal as if God himself commanded. And while they sit in their cells, intent on the work of their hands, on meditation and prayer, and apply their minds earnestly to these, if they hear someone knocking at the door of the cell to call them either to common prayer or to manual work, they at once leave everything and hasten to the task commanded, cultivating most zealously the virtue of obedience; which they set above not only manual work, reading, and quiet dwelling in the cell, but also above all the virtues, and they put everything after it.

6. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 13–16.) It is superfluous to mention that none of them possesses anything other than a *colobium* [sleeveless tunic], a *hemiphorium* [short cloak], sandals, a *melota* [sheepskin], and a mat: it is held shameful if anyone says 'my book', 'my writing-brush', or 'my' anything else. Each of them brings the monastery such income from his work and sweat that it suffices not only for their own needs but also for the service of guests and the poor. Yet while they labour thus, they are not puffed up, they do not swell with pride, nor does anyone, on account of his own labour and sweat, ask for more than the abbot assigns him for his need; nor does he acquire the possession of anything, since he regards himself as a stranger and pilgrim in the whole world, and considers himself rather the servant and minister of the brothers than the lord of any earthly place. If anyone breaks or loses any vessel, he confesses the mishap of his negligence to the abbot, and so with humility receives pardon through penance. But if anyone called to some work or to the *synaxis* comes too late out of contempt, or answers harshly and insolently; or if he carries out the order carelessly or with murmuring, or if, putting reading before manual work and obedience, he is too slow in completing the tasks ordered him, or, when dismissed from the assembly, does not hurry quickly to his work, or talks with someone without necessity, or boldly touches another's hand, or meets with relatives without the abbot's permission and blessing, or dares to receive a letter from anyone or write back to anyone without the abbot's leave; if, I say, he offends in any such matter, he is subjected to this penalty: when the brothers are gathered at the *synaxis*, he throws himself on the ground and, having confessed, asks pardon for his sin. But if anyone is caught committing graver offences, which are contempt, resistance with pride, or going out of the monastery without the abbot's leave, or meeting with a woman, or anger, or fighting, or enmity toward anyone, or remembering injuries, or love of money, which is the leprosy of the soul, or the possession of anything whatever except what the abbot gives, or food taken stealthily without the abbot's blessing, and things like these, he undergoes not the aforesaid penalty but a heavier and much greater one. And if he does not amend, he is expelled from the monastery.

7. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 17, 18.) That reading is held in some communities at mealtime is observed not from the rule of the Egyptians but from that of the Cappadocians, who established it not so much for the sake of spiritual exercise as for quiet and to avoid conversation. Among the Egyptians, however, and above all among the Tabennesiots, such silence is kept by all when that huge multitude of brothers gathers at table at mealtime that scarcely anything like it could be found; so much so that no one dares even to clear his throat, except the one in charge of the table, who, if anything is needed, signals it by knocking rather than by voice. They wear their hoods drawn down even below the eyelids, so that they do not look curiously at others with wandering eyes, and they apply their minds only to the table and to giving thanks to God who feeds them. And they take great care that none of them takes food outside the table.

8. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 19–21.) So that we may not seem to leave out anything of the cenobitic rules, we must also mention the rules handed down in other regions. Throughout Mesopotamia, Palestine and Cappadocia, and in the whole East, at the time of the assembly of the third, sixth and ninth hours, if anyone has not arrived before the first psalm is finished, he does not dare enter the oratory or join those singing the psalms, but waits, standing before the doors, for the brothers to be dismissed. Then, as they all come out, he lies prostrate on the ground, doing penance, and asks pardon for his negligence. At the night assemblies, however, pardon is granted to latecomers up to the second psalm. Further, the brothers succeed one another by weeks in the kitchen and in the other duties, both to lighten one another's labour and to fulfil the law of charity by mutual services. And they perform these ministries with such humility and care as not even slaves show toward their masters. When the week is completed, on the Lord's day after the morning hymns, they hand over the vessels of their office, sealed, to the others who are entering on service; and the others, having received them, guard them with such care and attentiveness that none of them is broken or lost, as great as one would show to whom sacred vessels dedicated to God are entrusted. For they prepare themselves to render account not only to the steward in the present time but also to God in the future, if any of them is lost through negligence or sloth. And for greater confidence in what has been said, I will relate what I saw with my own eyes. During a certain brother's week the steward, passing by, saw a few grains of lentil thrown on the ground, and did not disregard it as a thing of no value; but after rebuking at length the brother to whom that week had been entrusted, he punished him with a penalty, as one careless of things dedicated to God and trampling on his own conscience. For they keep and manage everything with such care and attentiveness that they guard with great attention things that seem to us cheap and contemptible; so that they move a vessel badly placed and pick up one thrown down, believing that they will receive a reward from the Lord God for these things too. We found these rules of the weeks observed throughout the whole East. Among the Egyptians, however, the rotation of weeks is not kept in this way; rather the care of the kitchen is entrusted to one of the most approved brothers, for as long, that is, as his virtue grows, his bodily strength suffices for performing the office, and neither old age nor infirmity prevents it. And since our discourse is about obedience and humility, by which we can reach the highest summit of virtue, I think it worthwhile to add to our account, by way of example, a few out of the many deeds splendidly done by the holy Fathers who shone in the communities.

9. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 27, 28.) There was a certain man named Patermutus, who, wishing to renounce the world, came to a community and persisted a long time before the doors of the monastery, until, because of his great patience, he was admitted with his small son, contrary to the usual law of the monastery. And when he had entered after many hardships, not only were both assigned to different tasks, but they were also separated in the dwelling of their cells, so that by that separation they might gradually be freed from their natural affection for each other; and from it, by the grace of Christ, through much exercise, the father was indeed freed. To test and prove his virtue, the abbot once pretended to be roused to anger against the boy, and ordered his aforesaid father to pick him up and throw him into the river. Then he, as though God were ordering him to take up his son, came running at speed to the bank of the river, and while he was hastening out of burning faith and fervour of obedience to fulfil the command, he was stopped by brothers who had gone ahead of him and snatched the son away. So acceptable to God was his faith and obedience that it was revealed by God to the abbot that he had accomplished the very work of Abraham. A short time afterwards, when the aforesaid abbot of the community died, he left him as his successor.

10. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapter 29.) We knew another brother who renounced the world, who had also been distinguished in the world (for his father was a count waging war, and rich), and was not moderately learned and devoted to reading. This man, then, having left behind worldly pomp, betook himself to the monastic life; and to test his faith and humility he was ordered by the abbot to carry ten baskets and to sell them in his own city, not all at once but one by one; which he carried out with all patience and humility, and putting the baskets on his shoulders he sold them one at a time; he took no account of the meanness of the task nor of the nobility of his birth, for he was striving to become an imitator of Christ's humility.

11. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 30–32.) Likewise we saw another of the fathers, Abba Pinufius, a man adorned with every virtue, who was old and abbot of a great community situated in Egypt near the city of Panephysis. When he saw himself praised and celebrated by all, both for his way of life and for his old age and office, and that he could not exercise himself in humility as at the beginning of his conversion, moved by this, for the sake of the subjection he longed for, in which he had been called, he fled secretly from his community and withdrew alone to the furthest parts of the Thebaid; and having taken off the monk's habit and put on secular clothes, he sought out the community of the Tabennesiots, thinking that he could lie hidden there, both because of the multitude of brothers and because it was far from the region in which his own community was situated. There, after he had begged for many days, he was received by the archimandrite, who, since he was old and useful for nothing else, gave him the care of the garden, together with another brother, to whom he was subject, and so cultivated the humility and obedience he longed for. Nor, content with that ministry alone, did he leave undone whatever tasks seemed hard and difficult to others, but carried them out eagerly. When he had passed three years hidden in this way, searched for by his disciples throughout all Egypt, he was at last, with difficulty, recognised by a certain brother who had come there, and who, on seeing him and recognising the shape of his face, being still in doubt, tried to hear his voice; for he was not certain from sight alone, having seen an old man digging the earth with a hoe and carrying dung on his shoulders to put at the roots of the vegetables. When, then, by observing the sound of his voice, he discovered who he was, he threw himself at his feet and struck the onlookers with great amazement, that he should behave so toward a man who was held among them as a novice, having left the world not long before, and the lowest of all. And they were more amazed when they learned his name, for he had previously been of great fame among them; and they asked pardon because in ignorance they had placed him among the last of the novices. And urging him with many words, they sent him back against his will to his own community, lamenting that he had not been allowed to exercise the humility and obedience he loved. So after spending a short time in his monastery, burning again with desire for humility and obedience, he watched for an hour of the night and fled, no longer to a distant region; for having boarded a small boat he came to the parts of Palestine, hoping that he could lie hidden there to the end. When he had arrived in Palestine, he sought out a monastery situated near the cave in which Christ the Lord was born, in which monastery he then stayed. But he could not lie hidden there, according to that saying of the Lord: A city set on a mountain cannot be hidden (Matth. 5:14). For when brothers had come from Egypt to venerate the holy places, they recognised him and, persuading him with many entreaties and tears, led him back again to his own community. With this saint, then, I lived for a short time in Egypt; and I will end my discourse by relating what I heard from him as he admonished a brother whom he admitted in my presence.

12. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 33–35.) You know, brother, he said, after how many days spent before the gate of the monastery you have been admitted today: if you learn the reason for such difficulty, it can bring you profit on this way which you desire to enter, and make you a faithful servant of God. For as glory and honour are promised in the future to those who serve the Lord faithfully, so the heaviest punishments threaten those who approach that promise softly and sluggishly. For it is better, according to Scripture, not to make a vow than not to fulfil one made. And again it is said: Cursed is he who does the work of the Lord negligently (Jer. 48:10). For this reason we repulsed you and delayed admitting you, not because we do not desire your salvation and that of all who believe in Christ, but lest, by admitting you rashly and without trouble, we ourselves should pay to God the penalty of excessive leniency, even [while] praying, and should make you liable to a heavier punishment, if we admitted you easily now, before you had learned the weight and exactness of the promise, and you afterwards turned out soft and sluggish. Therefore, as was said above, you must learn the reason for your renunciation, that is, what you must do. Renunciation, then, is nothing other than the promise of the cross and of death. Know therefore that from this day you are dead and crucified to the world, and the world to you, according to the Apostle; and learn what the power of the cross is: since you no longer live, but he lives in you who was crucified for you. In this pattern, then, in which the Lord was hung for us, we too must live in the community, as blessed David prays when he asks that his flesh be pierced through with the fear of the Lord (Ps. 118:120). For just as one whose body is fastened to wood is immovable for any action, so one who has his thought fastened by divine fear is immovable toward every carnal desire. And just as one fixed to a cross no longer thinks of present things, is not directed by his own will, is not troubled by desire, is not held by care for possessing, is not puffed up by pride, does not burn with contention or envy, does not grieve at present insult, does not remember past injuries, for he expects in a little while the end of his life, namely through the cross; so one who has sincerely renounced the world, and is fixed as on a cross by the fear of God, expecting daily the end of this life, holds all desires and all carnal affections immovable and powerless.

13. (Cassian, Institutes, book IV, chapters 36, 37.) Beware, then, lest you ever desire to take up again the things you gave up in your renunciation. For according to the Lord's sentence: He who puts his hand to the plough and turns back is not fit for the kingdom of heaven (Luke 9:62), and he who descends from a lofty way of life to the cheap and earthly things of this world acts against the Lord's command, when he comes down from the house and tries to take something out of the house. Beware, therefore, lest, remembering your old affection for your carnal parents and turning to the cares of this world, you be found, according to the Lord's word, not fit for the kingdom of heaven (Matth. 5:19). Beware lest you rouse again in yourself the pride which at the beginning you trampled down through the fervour of humility. When you have learned the psalter, or something of Scripture; or, according to the Apostle's word, when you build up again what you destroyed, [beware] lest you show yourself a transgressor; but rather, as you began and professed humility, keep it before God and his angels to the end. Likewise take care to increase the humility you showed at the monastery, when you persisted for many days before the monastery doors, supplicating with tears. It would be a thoroughly wretched thing if, when you ought daily to add to your fervour and ascend to perfection by constant progress, you should diminish and fall back to lower things. For not he who begins to do good is blessed, but whoever perseveres in it to the end. For the serpent, which drags itself along the ground, always watches our heel, that is, lays snares for our death, and tries to trip us up to the end of our life. Therefore it will profit nothing to have begun well, nothing [to have] a fervent beginning of obedience, unless a like end follows. And the humility according to Christ which you have now promised will not be made firm unless you show it to the end. Wherefore, so that you may possess it perfectly and crush the dragon's head (Gen. 3:15), when thoughts assail you, reveal them promptly, right from the beginning: for if you thus make known from the beginning the dragon's pernicious thoughts, if you are not ashamed to declare them to your father, you will crush his head. Indeed, according to divine Scripture, if you come to serve God, prepare yourself (Ecclus. 2:1), not for carelessness, not for idleness, but for temptations, for tribulations: for through many tribulations we must enter the kingdom of heaven (Acts 14:22), and narrow is the gate and strait the way that leads to life, and few there are who find it (Matth. 7:14). So turn your mind to those few good men, and shape your life by their example; and pay no attention to the lazy and the scornful, however many they may be: For many, he says, are called, but few chosen (Matth. 20:16); and it is a little flock to which it pleased the Father to give the kingdom (Luke 12:32). For do not think it a small sin to promise perfection and to imitate the more negligent and sluggish. So that you may be able to reach perfection, then, use this method; climb by these steps.

14. (Cass. Inst. bk. IV, ch. 39, 40.) The first step of virtue and the beginning of our salvation is the fear of God; for through it comes the cleansing of sins, and the guarding of the virtues and the way to perfection are obtained. For when the fear of God has entered the soul, it urges us to despise all worldly things; from this arises forgetfulness of kinsfolk and of the whole world. From these, further, humility is practised, the head of all virtues and the completion of all good things; for humility comes from contempt and deprivation of all things. Humility is proved by these signs: first, if one has his own wishes mortified in himself; second, if he hides nothing from his father, not only of his deeds but also of his thoughts; third, if he does not trust his own prudence, but in all things the discernment of his father, and always thirsts for, longs for, and gladly listens to his admonitions; fourth, if he carries out all his father's commands without shame; fifth, if not only does he not dare to inflict insults on another, but receives with joy those inflicted by others; sixth, if he undertakes to do nothing new that neither the common rule nor the examples of the Fathers permit; seventh, if, content with every lowliness, he gives thanks for the things given to him and thinks himself unworthy of them; eighth, if he thinks himself plainly inferior to all, and is not rash in words [Cassian, ibid.: Ninth, if he restrains his tongue, or is not loud in voice]; tenth, if he is not ready in speech and hasty of tongue. By these and similar signs humility is recognised; when these have truly been shown, they quickly lead to the summit of love, in which there is no fear of Gehenna, and through which all things are accomplished no longer from necessity and with toil, but from fervent love and from desire for the good. So that you may more easily attain this virtue, let the words of the brothers who run the course along with you and possess piety be your example; but not of those who, though more in number, spend their lives more negligently and sluggishly. For from the imitation and emulation of the saints great benefit comes to those who wish to strive toward perfection.

15. (Cass. Inst. bk. IV, ch. 41-43.) If, then, you wish to have the ability to carry out all these things, and under them to persevere to the end in the spiritual contest of the community, you will need for your guarding, in the company of the brothers, what David says: But I, like a deaf man, did not hear, and like a man who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth (Ps. 37:14). So whenever you see anything foreign to edification and profit, be as if blind; and if you hear anything like these things, become as if deaf and dumb, and having no rebukes in your mouth. And do not imitate those who are unfaithful, disobedient, insolent, scurrilous, insulting: but pass these things by as if dumb and not hearing. If anyone heaps reproaches, abuse, insults upon you, be unmoved as if bridled, and as if dumb; repeat this verse of the psalm to yourself constantly: I said, I will guard my ways, so that I do not sin with my tongue. I set a guard on my mouth, when the sinner stood against me. I was dumb and was humbled (Ps. 38:1). Besides these things, meditate above all on that fourth thing also; and observe what will be able to adorn those three things said above: namely, that you make yourself foolish and senseless in this world, according to the Apostle's precept, so that you may be wise (1 Cor. 3:18); that is, judging or doubting nothing in whatever is commanded you, being equipped, that is, with the simplicity and faith of obedience. Among all holy things, believe that alone to be holy, that wise, that profitable, which has been commanded you by your father. If you strengthen your heart in this purpose, you will be able to bear the yoke of Christ's obedience to the end, and none of the devil's temptations and arts will be able to shake you from the knowledge of life. Do not expect to establish your patience, humility, and equanimity from the virtue of others: that is, if no one goads you, no one despises you, no one disgraces you; for this is surely neither a proof of your virtue nor in your power; but [it is] if you bear reproaches, insults, and contempt willingly, for that is within your own choice. So, to say now in brief what we said more fully above, so that you may remember it more easily, hear again how you can reach perfection step by step. The beginning of our salvation is the fear of God; from it is born good obedience; from this arises submission and contempt for the things of the world; from this humility is born the mortification of one's own wishes; from the mortification of one's own wishes the roots of pleasures are dried up; and by these all the imperfections of the soul are driven out, at whose expulsion the virtues grow and bear fruit; from the increase of the virtues is born purity of heart; purity of heart is followed by apostolic perfection, by the grace and help of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ages of ages, amen.
BOOK TWO. ON THE EIGHT THOUGHTS OF WICKEDNESS.

1. (Cass. Inst. bk. V, ch. 1 ff.) Having first spoken about the constitution of monasteries, relying on your prayers we now undertake to write about the eight thoughts of wickedness, namely gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, sloth, vainglory, and pride. First, then, we shall speak of abstinence, which is opposed to gluttony: we shall also treat of the manner of fasts, and of the quality and quantity of foods. And we shall say these things not from ourselves, but [say] what we have received from our holy Fathers. They, then, did not hand down one rule of fasting, nor one manner of eating, nor the same measure for all, because not all are of the same strength or age, and because some suffer from bodily weakness, others have a more delicate body. But they handed down one aim for all: that they flee excess and shun a full belly; and they said it had been proved by experience that a daily fast is more useful, and contributes more to purity, than if the fast is prolonged to three or four days, or even to a week. For they say that one who prolongs his fast immoderately often takes food beyond measure; so that it often happens from this that sometimes the body falls into weakness from excessive abstinence and becomes more sluggish for spiritual services, and sometimes, on the contrary, burdened with a multitude of foods, it produces sloth and softness of mind. Again, [they say] that the use of vegetables does not suit everyone, nor likewise of pulses, and that a diet of dry bread cannot suffice for all; likewise that there are some who are still hungry after eating two pounds of bread, and others who are satisfied with one pound, or indeed six ounces. So to all, as has been said, they handed down one aim of abstinence: that they not be deceived by fullness of belly nor drawn by the pleasure of the palate. For not only difference of quality but also a great quantity of food tends to kindle the fiery darts of sin. For with whatever food the belly is filled, it begets the seeds of lust. And again, not only drunkenness from wine but also a surfeit of water, and an excess of any foods, weighs a man down and makes him torpid and drowsy. For the Sodomites the cause of their overthrow was not drunkenness from wine nor from various foods, but fullness of bread, according to the prophet (Ezek. 16:49). Weakness of body is not opposed to purity of heart. So give the body what its weakness requires, not what pleasure seeks. The use of food is employed as far as is necessary to sustain life, not so as to serve the impulse of desire. A moderate and reasonable taking of food secures the health of the body and does not take away holiness. This is the exact norm and rule of abstinence, handed down by the holy Fathers: that the one who eats should stop taking food while appetite still remains. And the Apostle, when he says: Make no provision for the flesh in its desires (Rom. 13:14), did not forbid the care necessary for life, but forbade the care of fostering pleasure. Moreover, for perfect purity of soul abstinence from food alone is not enough, unless the other virtues join with it. Humility, then, through obedience in work and through affliction of the body, confers great goods on us. To be free of avarice is this: not only not to have money, but not even to desire its possession. Restraint of anger, sadness, vainglory, and pride brings the soul to purity. All these produce the whole purity of the soul. But that particular purity of the soul which is obtained through temperance is produced above all by abstinence and fasting. For it is impossible for one who has a full belly to fight in spirit against the spirit of fornication. So let our first contest be to rule the belly and bring the body into subjection: not only through fasting, but also through vigils, labour, reading, and likewise by conceiving in the mind fear of Gehenna and desire for the kingdom of heaven.

2. (Cass. Inst. bk. VI, ch. 1 ff.) Our second contest is against the spirit of fornication and the desire of the flesh, a desire which begins to trouble a man from his earliest age. That is a great and heavy contest, consisting of a double struggle; for it is double, since it is waged in the body and in the soul. Therefore one must fight against it with a double battle. For bodily fasting is not enough for the possession of perfect temperance and for true chastity, unless there is also constant prayer to God, frequent meditation on the divine Scriptures, labour and the work of the hands, which can check the unstable impulses of the soul and call it back from obscene thoughts. Humility of soul contributes to this especially, without which no one will be able to overcome either fornication or the other passions. First of all, then, one must keep the heart with all vigilance from foul thoughts (Prov. 4:23). For from it, according to the Lord's word, come evil thoughts, murders, adulteries, fornications, and the rest (Matth. 15:19). For fasting has been enjoined on us not only for the affliction of the body, but also for the temperance of the mind, lest, darkened by a multitude of foods, it be unable to guard against thoughts. So we must devote all care not only to bodily fasting, but also to attention to our thoughts and to spiritual meditation, without which it is impossible to climb to the peak of true chastity and purity. It is fitting, then, according to the Lord's word, that we cleanse the inside of the cup and dish, so that the outside may be clean (Matth. 23:26). Therefore, if we are concerned, according to the Apostle, to contend lawfully and receive the crown (2 Tim. 2:5) by conquering the impure spirit of fornication, let us not trust in our own strength nor in our own ascetic practice, but in the help of the Lord God. For a man has no end of the contest with such a demon until he truly believes that he is freed from such a disease, and climbs to the highest summit of chastity, not by his own effort or labour, but by the prompting and help of God. For it is something above nature, and in a certain way he exists outside the body, who has trampled on the goads of the flesh and its pleasures. Therefore it is impossible for a man to fly up on his own wings, so to speak, to this peak and to the prize of holiness, and to become an imitator of the angels, unless the grace of God leads him out of the earth and the mire. For by no virtue do men bound in the flesh become more like the heavenly angels than by temperance: for through it, while still dwelling on earth, they have, according to the Apostle, their citizenship in heaven (Phil. 3:20). And this is the sign that this virtue has been acquired by us: if no image of obscene fantasy enters the mind while asleep. For even if such a movement is not counted as sin, it is nevertheless a sign of a soul that is sick and not yet freed from such a passion. Therefore we ought to regard those obscene fantasies occurring during sleep as proof of preceding sluggishness and of our weakness, and the end of the dream on waking reveals the disease lying hidden in the secret of our heart. That is why the physician of souls placed the remedy in the inner recesses of the soul, knowing the causes of the disease to be there, when he says: Whoever looks at a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart (Matth. 5:28), not only to correct wanton and curious eyes, but much more the soul situated within, which has wickedly used the eyes given it by God for good. This is the reason why the Wise man says in the proverb, not, Keep your eyes with all vigilance, but, Keep your heart with all vigilance (Prov. 4:23). That is, he applies the remedy of vigilance chiefly to that which uses the eyes at its own will. So let this be the first safeguard of our purification: that when the memory of a woman enters our mind through the devil's working, even of a mother, or a sister, or other pious women, we cast it quickly out of our heart; lest, if we linger too long in such a thought, that seducer and author of evils roll and hurl the mind down from the fantasy of such faces into obscene and harmful thoughts; just as is commanded in that command of God given to the first man, that he should watch the head of the serpent, that is, the beginning of the harmful thought by which it tries to creep into our soul, so that, having let in the head, that is, the first onset of the thought, we do not let in the rest of the serpent's body, namely the consent of pleasure, and from this he finally throws the mind down into a wicked deed. But it is right, as it is written, to slay in the morning all the sinners of the land (Ps. 100:8); that is, by the light of knowledge to discern and destroy the thoughts leading to sin; out of the land, that is, out of the heart, according to the Lord's word. And while the children of Babylon (Ps. 136:9), that is, evil thoughts, are still little, then we must level them to the ground and dash them against the rock, which is Christ. For if by our consent they reach manhood, they will not be overcome without great groans and labours. To what has been said above from sacred Scripture must be added the sayings of the holy Fathers. It was said, then, by Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia: I do not know woman, and yet I am not a virgin; so thoroughly had he ascertained that the gift of virginity is rightly possessed not by bodily abstinence from woman alone, but is customarily had much more by holiness and purity of soul and by the fear of God. The Fathers also say that we cannot possess the virtue of perfect chastity unless we first possess true humility in the heart; nor are we held worthy of true knowledge as long as the affection of fornication lies in the inner recesses of the soul. And to make plain the greatness of such a virtue from the Apostle himself, let us recall one sentence of his, with which we will end our speaking. Pursue peace, he says, with all, and holiness, without which no one will see the Lord (Heb. 12:14). For that he speaks about this matter is plain from what he added, when he says: Lest anyone be a fornicator or profane, like Esau (ibid.). So the more heavenly and angelic the virtue of chastity is, the heavier the snares with which it is attacked by the enemy. Therefore we must take care not only to keep bodily temperance, but also to pour out contrition of heart and frequent prayers with groans; so that the furnace of our flesh, which the Babylonian king kindles daily with the goads of desire, may be quenched by the dew of the presence of the Holy Spirit. Besides this, a very great weapon is at hand for us against such an enemy, namely vigils kept in God. For just as chastity and watchfulness by day prepare holiness by night, so vigils in God by night [prepare holiness] by day...

3. (Cassian, Inst. Book 7, ch. 1 and following.) Our third contest is against the spirit of avarice. This war is a foreign one, and is found to lie outside nature, and it befalls a monk through the occasion of unbelief. For the goads of the other passions, namely anger and desire, seem to take their occasion from the body; they are in a way implanted, and have their beginning from birth, which is why they are overcome only over a long time. But the disease of avarice, coming from outside, can be cut out more easily, provided there is care and attention of mind. If it is neglected, however, it is more destructive than the other passions and becomes accursed, for according to the Apostle it is the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6:10). Let us consider these things in this way. The natural movements of the body are seen not only in boys, in whom there is as yet no discernment of good and evil, but even in the very smallest infants at the breast, who, though they have not even a trace of carnal pleasure, still show movement in the flesh. Likewise the goad of anger appears in infants, when we see them stirred up against those who cause them annoyance. I say this not to accuse nature as the cause of sin, far from it, but to show that, although anger and desire were given to man by God the Creator for good, man nevertheless seems in some way to slip, through his own sloth, from the nature of the body into what is against nature. For the movement of the body was given by the Creator for the procreation of children and the continual succession of the human race, not for fornication; and the stirring of anger was implanted in us for our salvation, so that we may be angry against sin, not so that we may be roused to fury against one of our own kind. If, then, we use these wrongly, nature in no way sins on that account, nor should we on that account accuse the maker; just as we should not accuse one who gave iron for a necessary and useful purpose, if the one who received it uses it to commit murders. We have said this to show that the passion of avarice does not take its beginning from a natural movement, but from wickedness alone and from a corrupt will. For when this disease finds a soul lukewarm and unbelieving at the start of its withdrawal, it suggests certain just causes, reasonable at least in appearance, to persuade it to keep back something of its possessions. It presents to the monk's mind a long old age and weakness of body: that what is given for need in the monastery is not enough for comfort, not only for one who is sick but not even for one who is well; that no proper care of the sick is taken there, but they are much neglected, so that if one has no gold secretly at hand, one must perish miserably. Finally it suggests that one cannot persevere long in the monastery because of the heaviness of the work and the severity of the father. And when it has primed his mind with such thoughts, so that he keeps back even a single denarius, it then persuades him to learn a craft without the abbot's knowledge, by which he can increase the money he has carefully hoarded. At last it deceives the wretch with a secret hope, suggesting the profit that will come to him from his craft, and that from this there will be rest and a mind free from cares. And at last, bound up in the thought of gain, he considers nothing adverse: not how great his anger will be, how great his fury, if he happens to suffer some loss; how great his gloom, how great his grief, if he is deprived of the profit of his work. But just as for others the belly is their god, so for him is gold. Therefore, since blessed Paul knew this well, he called it not only the root of all evils, but also idolatry. Let us weigh, then, into how great a wickedness this disease drags a man, since it casts him into idolatry. For once the avaricious man has torn his mind away from the love of God, he loves the images of men engraved on gold. And the monk darkened by such thoughts, as he grows towards worse things, can thereafter have no humility, no obedience; but he is angry, he is indignant, he grumbles at every task, he resists, and at last, keeping no shame at all, he is carried like a wholly unbridled horse over the cliffs; and, not content with his daily food, he finally declares that he cannot bear it any longer. He says that God is not there only, and that his salvation is not shut up in that place, but that God is found everywhere by those who seek him; that he will perish unless he leaves that monastery. And so, since the hidden money is at hand to aid his corrupt mind, as if lifted up on wings, and planning his departure from the monastery, he thereafter answers every order proudly and harshly, and, regarding himself as a stranger and outsider, if he sees anything in the monastery deserving correction, he does not care at all, indeed he despises it. Then he looks for occasions of anger or complaint, so that he may not seem to leave the monastery lightly and without cause. Nor does he hesitate to behave in such a way as to find an abettor of his offence. So the avaricious man, led astray by the fire of his money, can never be at rest in the monastery or live under the rule. And when the demon has snatched him from the fold like a wolf and, having separated him from the fold, has taken him to devour, it then sees to it that the works which he utterly neglected at the set hours in the monastery he performs night and day with great eagerness in his own cell; and it does not let him keep the custom of prayers, the practice of fasts, the rule of vigils, but, once he is bound up in the fury of avarice, persuades him to spend all his zeal and all his labour on his work. There are three forms of this disease, all equally forbidden by the divine Scriptures and the teaching of the Fathers. The first, of which we wrote above, sees to it that wretched men acquire and pile up things which they did not have even in the world. The second works so that those who have renounced their money repent of it, and persuades them to demand back what they offered to God. The third is the one which, having first bound the monk in the lukewarmness of unbelief, does not let him renounce worldly things perfectly, suggesting to his mind fear of poverty and distrust of God's providence, and shows him to be a violator of his promises, namely of what he professed when he renounced the world. We find examples of these three forms hidden in the divine Scripture. For Gehazi, because he desired money which he had not had before, was deprived of the grace of prophecy which his master wished to leave him as an inheritance; and instead of a blessing he acquired, through the prophet's curse, an everlasting leprosy (4 Kgs. 5). Judas, wishing to take back the money which he had earlier thrown away in order to follow the Lord, not only was thrust out of the company of the Apostles when he had turned his mind to betraying the Lord, but ended his very bodily life by a violent death (Matt. 27:5). Ananias and Sapphira, when they kept back some of what they had consecrated to the Lord, paid the penalty of death at the apostle's word (Acts 5). And the great Moses in Deuteronomy gives a mystical precept to those who are about to renounce the world and still cling to earthly things out of a certain fear born of distrust: If any man is timid and fearful at heart, he shall not go out to war; let him go home and live softly there, lest he strike fear into the hearts of his brothers (Deut. 20:8). Is there anything safer and clearer than this testimony? Do we not learn from these words that we who renounce the world must renounce it perfectly and so go forward to war, lest by a soft and corrupt beginning we turn others away from the perfection of the Gospel? And since that which is rightly said in Scripture, It is more blessed to give than to receive (Acts 20:35), some interpret badly, doing violence to the letter and twisting the sense of the saying to their own deceit and to the desire for money, as also the Lord's teaching, which runs thus: If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor, and you will have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me (Matt. 19:21); and they judge the means of wealth to be happier than poverty, and that out of such abundance they can give generously to the needy: let such men know that they have not yet renounced the world, nor are they walking in monastic perfection, so long as they are ashamed to take up for Christ, with the Apostle, a glorious poverty, and to provide for themselves and the needy by the work of their hands. But if they desire to fulfil the monastic promise in deed and to receive glory with the Apostle, let them distribute their former riches and fight the good fight with Paul in hunger, thirst and nakedness (2 Tim. 4:7). For if the Apostle himself had thought the possession of former riches necessary for perfection, he would by no means have despised his former rank; for he testifies that he was a distinguished man and a Roman citizen (Acts 22:25). And those in Jerusalem who sold their houses and estates and laid [the proceeds] at the feet of the apostles (Acts 4:35) would never have done so if they had known that the apostles thought it happier to be fed by one's own money than by one's own labour and the work of one's hands. The Apostle teaches this matter more clearly in his Epistle to the Romans: But now I shall go to Jerusalem to minister to the saints. For Macedonia and Achaia have thought it good to make some contribution for the poor among the saints who are in Jerusalem (Rom. 15:25). And he himself, often in chains and in prisons, and subject to the hardships of travel, and so prevented from providing his necessities with his own hands as he used to, shows that he received them from the brothers who were from Macedonia and who had come to him, saying: For what I lacked the brothers who came from Macedonia supplied (2 Cor. 11:9). And to the Philippians: That at the beginning of the Gospel I shared with no church in the matter of giving and receiving except with you alone; for in Thessalonica too you served my needs once and twice (Phil. 4:15). So, by their own reasoning, let the avaricious be more blessed than the Apostle, since they are supplied with what they need from their own substance. But no one, unless he had fallen into the utmost madness, would dare to say that. If, then, we wish to follow the precept of the Gospel and the apostles, and the whole Church founded from the beginning upon the apostles, let us not obey our own opinions, nor misunderstand what has been rightly said, but, rejecting that lukewarm and unbelieving disposition of mind, let us pursue a careful zeal for the Gospel. For in this way we shall be able to follow the footsteps of the holy Fathers, and never to depart from the knowledge and institution of the monastery, and likewise truly to renounce this world. It will be worthwhile at this point to recall the sayings of the holy Fathers. There is reported a saying of Saint Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to a certain man of senatorial rank who renounced the world lukewarmly and kept back something of his money; the saying was this: You have both lost the senator and not made the monk. We must therefore with all care cut out of our soul the root and beginning of all evils, namely avarice, knowing for certain that while the root remains the branches sprout, and that it is difficult to practise virtue unless we live in a monastery, for in it we have no care even about necessary things. Keeping before our eyes the condemnation of Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), let us shudder at keeping back for ourselves anything of our former means. Likewise let us fear the example of Gehazi (4 Kgs. 5), who because of avarice was handed over to everlasting leprosy. Let us beware of piling up for ourselves the money of this life, which we did not possess even in this world. Let us likewise fear, considering Judas perishing by the noose, lest we keep back anything of all those things which we renounced with contempt. Besides all this, always keeping before our eyes the uncertain hour of death, let us beware lest the Lord come at an hour we do not expect and find our conscience stained with avarice, and say to us what was said to that rich man in the Gospel: Fool, this night they demand your soul from you; and the things you have prepared, whose will they be? (Luke 12:20)

4. (Cass. Inst. bk. 8, ch. 1 ff.) Our fourth contest is against the spirit of anger, so that with God we may cut out its deadly poison from the inmost part of our soul. For when it is lodged within our heart and blinds the eye of the mind with dark tumults, we are able to have no discernment of the things that are fitting for us, nor to find the grasp of spiritual knowledge, nor to be made partakers of true life, nor will our mind be capable of the divine and true light. For, it says, My eye is troubled by rage (Ps. 6:8). Nor shall we be partakers of wisdom, even if we seem wise to ourselves, since it is written: Rage will dwell in the bosom of fools; nor can we attain the saving rays of discernment, even if we are reckoned very wise by men, for it is written: Anger destroys even the prudent; nor can we hold the helm of justice with a watchful heart, since it is written: The anger of man does not work the justice of God (James 1:20); nor can we obtain the modesty and seemliness praised by the mouths of all, since it is written: An angry man is not modest (Prov. 11:25). So whoever wishes to attain perfection, whoever longs to engage lawfully in the spiritual contest, let him be a stranger to every fault of anger or rage, and let him hear what that Vessel of election commands: Let all bitterness and anger and indignation and clamour and blasphemy be removed from you, with all malice (Eph. 4:31). And when he says all, he has left us no occasion for indignation, whether as if necessary or as if fitting. So whoever wishes to rebuke an erring brother or to inflict correction on him, let him take care to keep himself free of agitation and disturbance, lest while he wishes to cure another he contract a disease himself, and that word of the Gospel be said to him: Physician, cure yourself (Luke 4:23); and again: Why do you see the speck in your brother's eye, but do not perceive the beam in your own eye? Or how will you say to your brother: Let me cast the speck out of your eye, you who have a beam in your own eye covering it (Matt. 7:3–4)? For for whatever reason the motion of anger boils up, it blinds the eyes of the mind and does not allow a man to look upon the Sun of justice. For just as one who lays gold or lead plates over his eyes equally hinders the faculty of sight, and the value of the gold makes no difference to the blinded, so, from whatever cause the agitation of anger is kindled, it darkens the soul's faculty of sight. We use indignation according to nature only when we move it against vicious and voluptuous thoughts. This indeed the prophet David teaches us when he says: Be angry and do not sin (Ps. 4:5); that is, move anger against your own passions and also against wicked thoughts, and do not sin by doing what they suggest to you. And what follows plainly declares this interpretation: What you say, it says, in your hearts, be pricked with compunction for it on your beds (ibid.); that is, when wicked thoughts have risen into your heart, cast them out, rousing your anger against them; and after they have been cast out, then, as if in bed or at rest, be pricked to repentance. With this blessed Paul agrees, who used the testimony of this saying and added: Let not the sun go down upon your anger; do not give place to the devil (Eph. 4:26); that is, do not, by consenting to wicked thoughts and provoking Christ the Sun of justice, cause him to set in your hearts, lest at his departure the devil find a place in you. Of this Sun God says through the prophet: To those who fear my name the Sun of justice will rise, and healing will be in his wings (Mal. 4:2). But if we take that saying (of the Apostle) literally, we are not permitted to keep anger even until sunset. What then shall we say of those who, corrupted by the savagery and madness of their feeling, not only keep anger until the setting of this sun, but even prolong it for many days, abstaining from speaking with one another; and no longer express their anger in words, but, keeping silence toward each other, kindle the poison of remembered injuries to their own ruin, not knowing that one must abstain not only from the sin committed in deed, but also from that conceived in the mind, lest the mind, darkened by the shadows of remembering injuries, fall from the light of knowledge and discernment and be deprived of the indwelling of the Holy Spirit. For this reason the Lord commands in the Gospels that the gift be left upon the altar and that one be reconciled to one's brother (Matt. 5:24), since it cannot be that the gift is accepted while we are occupied with anger and the memory of injuries. And the Apostle, when he says that we must pray without ceasing, and that holy hands must be lifted up in every place (1 Thess. 5:17), teaches that this must be done without anger, even if it is only in thought. It remains, then, either that we never pray, and so are liable under the apostolic precept, or, if we take care to keep the precepts, that we do it without anger and remembrance of injuries. But since it often happens that when brothers are saddened or disturbed we disregard the matter and say that we are not the cause of their sadness, the physician of souls, in order to tear up the occasions of anger by the roots from our heart, commands not only that, if we are saddened and angry with our brother, we leave the gift and be reconciled to him (Matt. 5:24), but also, if he is angry with us, rightly or wrongly, that we calm his anger by our apology, and then offer the gift. But why linger longer on the precepts of the Gospels and the Apostles, when this can also be learned from the old law, which, although it seems to bend away from that severity and adapt itself, says this: Do not hate your brother in your heart (Lev. 19:17); and again: The ways of those who keep the memory of injuries [lead] to death (Prov. 12:28). For in this place it forbids and punishes not only the anger that breaks out into deed, but also that which is kept in the mind. Therefore, holding fast to the divine laws, we must struggle with all our strength against the spirit of anger and against that disease situated within us, and not stir up anger against men, and for that reason pursue solitude and separation, so that, with no one present there to provoke us to anger, the virtue of equanimity may easily be exercised in solitude; for it comes both from pride and from our unwillingness to accuse ourselves and to ascribe the causes of anger to our own sluggishness that we long to be separated from the brothers. So long, then, as we impute the causes of our weakness to others, it is impossible for us to attain the perfection of equanimity. For the sum of our amendment is obtained not from our neighbour's equanimity toward us, but from our own long-suffering toward our neighbour and forgetting of injuries. And when, fleeing the contest of equanimity, we seek the desert and solitude, whatever passions we bring there not yet cured and calmed, let us consider them hidden, not destroyed. For the desert and retirement, for those not yet free of passions, know how not only to preserve imperfections but also to hide them. Nor do they allow them to perceive to what passions they are subject; rather, by the fancies they suggest, they persuade them that they have attained equanimity and humility, so long as no one is present to provoke and test them; but when an occasion arises by which they are provoked and exercised, the passions long stored up and hidden at once, like unbridled horses bursting out of their stables, well fed by long rest and idleness, hurl their rider to destruction all the more violently and wildly. For passions left in idleness and not stirred up by men grow wilder in us; and the very shadow of patience and equanimity, which we hold only in fancy and opinion, if we mix with the brothers, we lose through the idleness of solitude, by neglect of exercise. For just as venomous animals, lying in the desert and in their lairs, show their fury only when they catch someone approaching, so men subject to passions, being at rest not from a disposition of virtue but from the necessary condition of a deserted place, vomit out the poison of their soul when they have caught someone approaching and provoking them. Therefore it is entirely fitting that those who seek the perfection of meekness should be angry not only not against men, but not even against beasts, nay not even against inanimate things. I remember that when I was living in the desert I conceived anger against a reed pen, because now its thickness, now its thinness displeased me; likewise against a piece of wood, because when I wanted to cut it I could not do so quickly; and again against a flint, because when I was in a hurry to strike fire the spark did not leap out at once; so far indeed does anger rage that it is carried even against insensible and inanimate things. If, then, we desire to attain the beatitude of Christ, we must restrain not only the anger that breaks out into deed, as was said above, but also that which is conceived in the mind. For it does not bring as much benefit to restrain one's mouth and not utter some furious word as to cleanse the heart of the memory of injuries and not to cherish wicked thoughts. For the teaching of the Gospel teaches that the roots of sins must be cut out rather than the branches. For once the root of anger is cut from the heart, no hatred, no envy will be carried through into deed; for he who hates his brother is a murderer, since by the feeling of hatred he kills him. And God sees him slain: men do not see his blood shed by the sword, but he was slain by the feeling of hatred. God therefore will repay to each crowns or punishments not only for deeds but also for thoughts and intention, as he himself says through the prophet: I come to gather their works, thoughts and meditations. And again the Apostle says: Their thoughts among themselves accusing or else defending one another, on the day when God will judge the secrets of men (Rom. 2:15–16). And the Lord himself, teaching that we must lay aside all anger, says in the Gospels: Whoever is angry with his brother will be liable to judgement (Matt. 5:22). For so the accurate copies read; for that word 'without cause' is an addition, as is clear from the preceding clause of Scripture. For the Lord's aim is that we cut off the root and spark of anger entirely and keep not even the least occasion of anger within us, so that we may not, if we stir up anger on a reasonable ground, at last fall into the fury of a brutish spirit. Now the perfect remedy for this disease is this: that we be persuaded that it is not lawful for us to stir up our indignation for either a just or an unjust cause. For if the spirit of anger darkens our mind, neither the light of discernment nor the helm of right counsel and justice will be found in us; nor, while the spirit of anger rules, can our soul become a temple of the Holy Spirit. Finally, keeping before our eyes the uncertain hour of death, we must guard ourselves from anger, and know that neither ascesis nor temperance nor renunciation of every material thing nor fasts and vigils will be of benefit to us if, seized by anger and hatred, we are liable to judgement. From which may we be freed by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory for ever and ever.

5. (Cassian, Inst. book IX, ch. 1 and following.) Our fifth contest is against the spirit of sadness, which darkens our soul so that it cannot devote itself to any spiritual contemplation, and restrains it from every good work. For when that wicked spirit has seized the soul and darkened it wholly, it does not allow it to pour out prayers with eagerness, nor to devote itself to gaining profit from the sacred readings, nor does it let it be gentle and agreeable to the brothers: it suggests hatred of every task of zeal, and of the very profession of [this] life. In short, while sadness confounds all the soul's salutary counsels and dissolves its firmness and perseverance, it makes it as it were foolish and stunned, and at last binds it fast with the thought of despair. Therefore let us have one aim: to fight the spiritual fight, to conquer the spirits of wickedness with God, and with all vigilance to keep our heart from the spirit of sadness (Prov. 4:23). For as the moth [consumes] a garment and the worm wood, so sadness gnaws away a man's soul, persuading him to turn aside from all upright company, and not allowing him to accept counsel from true friends, nor to give them a mild and peaceable answer; rather, sadness throws the whole soul into turmoil and fills it with carelessness; and at last it persuades it to flee from men, as though they had been the cause of its disturbance; nor does it let it recognise that the sickness is seated not outside but within, and becomes apparent when assailing temptations bring it into the open by trial. For a man will never be harmed by another unless he has the disease seated within, namely the causes of the passions: which is why God, the maker of all and physician of souls, who alone knows the wounds of the soul rightly and exactly, does not command us to leave the company of men, but to cut out the causes of wickedness in us, knowing that the soul's health is not obtained by separation from men, but by living among men and by exercise. So when, on certain plausible occasions, we leave the brothers, we by no means cut off the occasions of sadness, but only exchange them, since the disease seated within stirs them up according to circumstances. Therefore let our whole war be against the inner passions. For when these have been cast out with God's help, we shall easily live, I do not say with men, but even with wild beasts, according to that saying of blessed Job: Savage beasts will be at peace with you (Job 5:23). First of all, then, we must fight against the spirit of sadness, which casts the soul into despair, so that we may drive that [evil] out of our heart. For it did not allow Cain to repent after his brother's murder, nor Judas after the betrayal of the Lord. Let us have only that sadness which looks to repentance for sins, joined with good hope, and which wins possession of heavenly goods; of which the Apostle said: The sadness that is according to God (2 Cor. 7:10)..... So that sadness which nourishes the soul with the hope of repentance is mixed with joy: therefore it makes a man eager and compliant for every good work, and also approachable and humble.
Here one leaf is missing, namely the rest of [the section] against the spirit of sadness and the beginning of what is said about the spirit of torpor.

6. (Cassian, Inst. book X, ch. 13 and following.) ...may eat bread. Let us hear how wisely the Apostle shows us the causes of this torpor. For he calls those who do not work disorderly (2 Thess. 3:6), declaring much wickedness by this single word. For he who is idle is also rash in words, and ready to revile, and in the end unfit to lead a quiet life, and a slave of torpor. He therefore commands that we withdraw, that is, separate ourselves from him as from a pestilent disease. Then what does he say? And not according to the tradition which they received from us (2 Thess. 3:6); and by this saying he shows that they are proud, contemptuous, and violators of the apostolic traditions. And again: Nor did we eat bread from anyone for nothing, he says, but in toil and weariness, working night and day, so as not to burden any of you (ibid., 8). That teacher of the Gentiles, herald of the Gospel, who was caught up to the third heaven (2 Cor. 12:2), who says that the Lord commanded that those who proclaim the Gospel should live by the Gospel (1 Cor. 9:14), worked in toil night and day so as not to burden anyone. What then shall we do, who out of torpor shun work and seek bodily rest; to whom neither the preaching of the Gospel nor the care of churches has been entrusted, but only the care of our own soul lies upon us? Then, showing more clearly how much harm comes from idleness, he adds: Doing no work, but being busybodies (2 Thess. 3:11); from idleness comes disorder, from disorder all wickedness arises. Then, preparing a remedy for this, he says: Now those who are such we charge and exhort, that working in silence they eat their own bread (ibid., 12), and with great rebuke he adds: If anyone will not work, let him not eat (ibid., 10). Taught by these apostolic precepts, the holy Egyptian fathers do not allow monks, especially the younger, to be idle for even the least time, knowing that by perseverance in work they drive out torpor, procure their own food, and help the needy. For they work not only for their own needs, but from their work they also supply necessities to strangers, the poor, those committed to prison, and all the needy; and they believe that a service of this kind is a sacrifice acceptable to God. The Fathers also say this: that he who works fights with one demon and is often troubled by it, but the idle man is the captive of countless demons. It will be worthwhile to recall a saying of Abba Moses, most eminent among the Fathers, which he spoke to me. For when I had been sitting in the desert a short time, torpor afflicted me, and going to him I addressed him thus: Grievously afflicted with torpor and much weakened, I was not freed from it until I went away and visited Abba Paul. Abba Moses answered me: Be well aware that you have by no means freed yourself from it so far; rather, you have handed yourself over to it as a surrendered captive and slave. Know therefore that, as a deserter, you will be warred down by it more heavily, unless from now on you strive to fight it by patience, prayer and the work of your hands.

7. (Cassian, Inst. book XI, ch. 1 and following.) Our seventh contest is against the spirit of vainglory, that many-formed and most subtle passion, which is not grasped even by the one who is tempted. For the assaults of the other passions are more open, and it is easier to fight with them: for the soul, when it recognises the war, overcomes by resisting and praying. But the wickedness of vainglory, since it is many-formed, as was said above, is hard to overcome. For it presents itself in every pursuit of a man: in dress, appearance, gait, speech, vigils, fasts, in prayer, reading, quiet, in equanimity. By all these it tries to stab the soldier of Christ. For whom it cannot deceive and turn to vainglory by costly clothing, him it tempts by cheapness of clothing. And whom it could not [puff up] by honour, him it puffs up to folly by the endurance of disgrace; whom it could not lead to vainglory by knowledge, him it tries to deceive through silence, as a man of quiet; whom it could not draw to softness by rich food, him it leads by fasting to the desire for praise. In short, every work, every pursuit gives this demon an occasion for war. Besides this, the one it assails sometimes imagines for himself the grades of holy orders. I remember a certain old man who, when I was living in Scetis, went to the cell of a certain brother to visit him, and as he approached the door of the cell he heard him talking inside; and since the old man thought he was repeating something from Scripture, he stood to listen, and perceived that he was raving from vainglory, ordaining himself deacon and giving the dismissal to the catechumens. When the old man heard this, he at last opened the door and went in; the brother, running to meet him, greeted him as usual and asked whether he had stood long at the door. Then the old man calmly answered him: I came just now, he said, when you were giving the dismissal to the catechumens. Hearing this, the brother fell at the old man's feet, to beg with prayers for deliverance from such an error. I have recalled this matter to show into what great folly this demon casts a man. So whoever wishes to contend perfectly and be crowned with the crown of justice, let him strive by every means to overcome this many-formed beast, always keeping before his eyes that saying of holy David: The Lord has scattered the bones of those who please men (Ps. 52:6); and let him do nothing with a view to human praise, but seek his reward from God, and always cast off thoughts of his own praise as they invade his heart; let him despise himself in the sight of God. For in this way he will be able, with God's help, to be freed from the demon of vainglory, by the grace of our Lord Jesus, to whom be glory for ever. Amen.

8. (Cassian, Inst. book XII, ch. 1 and following.) Our eighth contest is against the spirit of pride, which is heavier and fiercer than all the others; by it the perfect are most of all assailed, and it tries to overthrow those who have almost reached the summit of the virtues; and like a pestilential disease it destroys not a part of the body but the whole. The other passions, each of them, although they disturb the soul, yet because they fight only with the one virtue opposed to them and strive to overcome it, darken and disturb the soul only in part; but the passion of pride covers the whole [soul] with darkness and leads it to final ruin. And so that we may think out more clearly what has been said, let us consider the matter in this way. The vice of gluttony strives to corrupt abstinence, fornication continence, avarice poverty, indignation meekness, and the other kinds of wickedness the virtues contrary to them; but the wickedness of pride, when it rules a wretched soul, acts no differently from some most savage tyrant who, having taken a great and lofty city, demolishes the whole of it and overturns it from its foundations. Witness to this is the angel who fell from heaven because of pride; created by God and adorned with every virtue and wisdom, he would not ascribe these things to the grace of God but to his own nature; whence he thought himself equal to God. Reproving this thought of his, the prophet says: You said in your heart: I will sit on a lofty mountain, I will set my throne above the clouds, and I will be like the Most High (Isa. 14:13). But you are a man, and not God (ibid. 31:3). And another prophet says: Why do you glory in wickedness, you who are mighty? and after a few words: You have loved all words of drowning, a deceitful tongue. Therefore God will destroy you for ever, he will pluck you out and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living. The just will see and fear, and will laugh over him and say: Behold the man who did not make God his helper, and prevailed in his vanity (Ps. 51). Since we know these things, let us fear, and with all vigilance guard our heart (Prov. 4:23) from the deadly spirit of pride, repeating to ourselves these words of the Apostle whenever we have accomplished a work of any virtue: Yet not I, but the grace of God which is with me (1 Cor. 15:10); and what was said by the Lord: Without me you can do nothing (John 15:5); and what was said by the prophet: Unless the Lord builds the house, those who build it have laboured in vain (Ps. 126:1); and again: It is not of him who wills, nor of him who runs, but of God who shows mercy (Rom. 9:16). For even if someone is fervent with eagerness and zealous in his purpose, yet, bound as he is by flesh and blood, he will not be able to reach perfection unless in all these things he has hoped in the mercy and grace of Christ; for, according to the divine James: Every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (Jas. 1:17). And Paul says: For what do you have that you did not receive? And if you received it, why do you glory as if you had not received it (1 Cor. 4:7)? But you are puffed up about others' gifts as if they were your own. That salvation comes to us by the grace and mercy of God, that thief is witness, who obtained the kingdom of heaven not as the reward of virtue but by the grace and mercy of God (Luke 23:43). Since our fathers knew these things well, they all handed down with one opinion that we cannot lay a firm foundation for the perfection of virtue except through humility, which proceeds from faith, meekness and perfect poverty; by which perfect charity is obtained, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, with whom to the Father be glory, with the Holy Spirit, for ever. Amen.
